newsitem.title: USA: U.S. May retail sales drop for third straight month.
newsitem.headline: U.S. May retail sales drop for third straight month.

text.p: Sales at retail stores dropped for a third month in a row during May, the Commerce Department said on Thursday, partly reflecting weaker sales of costly durables like new cars.
Total retail sales dropped 0.1 percent last month to a seasonally adjusted $210.3 billion after revised drops of 0.9 percent in April and 0.3 percent in March.
It was the first time in more than 15 years that retail sales have weakened for three consecutive months, department officials said, possibly indicating a slowing of consumer demand.
The continued faltering in sales was a surprise, since Wall Street economists had forecast May sales would rebound to rise 0.4 percent instead of decline.

The inflation-sensitive U.S. Treasury bond market leaped after the report, with the benchmark 30-year bond up nearly a full point. Its yield, which moves in the opposite direction, fell to 6.77 percent from 6.84 percent Wednesday.
The department previously said April sales were down by a smaller 0.3 percent and that March sales had been flat, but it revised both of those estimates to show steeper decreases.
Commerce said the revised 0.9 percent decline in April sales was the biggest monthly fall-off in more than two years, since a 1.6 percent plunge in February 1995.

During May, sales by auto dealers fell 0.2 percent after a steeply revised 2 percent drop in April -- the steepest monthly decline in a year, since a 2.9 percent fall in April 1996. Previously, Commerce said April auto sales were down only 0.9 percent.
Some auto plants were closed by strikes in April and sales fell.
Auto manufacturers say spring sales of new cars have remained lackluster.

New cars account for nearly one-quarter of total retail sales, so swings in demand strongly affect the overall monthly figures. But even excluding cars, retail sales were down 0.1 percent in May after a 0.5 percent fall in April.

Another key point of weakness in May retail business was in building materials and hardware, which fell 0.6 percent to $12 billion after a 0.3 percent decline in April. New housing activity has leveled off after a spurt at the start of the year when mild weather fostered more building.

Total sales of durable goods fell 0.3 percent to $85.7 billion in May following a 1.2 percent plunge in April. Sales of more quickly used nondurables like food and paper products were flat at $124.6 billion after falling 0.6 percent in April.
Some segments of the retail industry were stronger in May.

Sales by general merchandise stores rose 0.7 percent to $27.3 billion after a 1 percent fall in April. At apparel stores, sales of clothing increased 0.8 percent to $9.6 billion after decreasing 0.5 percent in April.

The retail sales report is closely watched as a measure of the vigour of consumer demand, a key factor cited by the Federal Reserve in March when it raised short-term interest rates for the first time in more than two years by a quarter percentage point.
The Fed left rates unchanged at a subsequent May policy-makers' session. It meets again at the beginning of July to consider interest-rate strategy.

The continued falloff in retail sales suggests a weaker rate of economic expansion in the second quarter after a booming 5.8 percent annual rate of growth in national output during the first three months this year.
